title: California subpoenas Nvidia — and asks what investors were told
summary: California's attorney general subpoenas Nvidia over whether chips or secrets reached China and whether investors were misled, as Nvidia's quarterly risk disclosures run late. Then how the Claude Code team verifies code it no longer reads line by line, and the Y Combinator debate between Jacob Coxon and Robin Hanson on slowing frontier AI.

topics: California AG Rob Bonta investigative subpoena to Nvidia (19 Nov 2026): asks whether advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public; 'bright red flags'; 'our corporate securities law ... Companies cannot mislead their investors'; no statute, document list or deadline published; read against Nvidia's Oct 2025 Megaspeed statement and Oct 29 2026 'not unusual or unexpected' statement, the delayed 10-Q (UBS: tied to the investigation and possible added risk factors), WSJ-reported SEC probe; Huang before congressional committees Dec 1, GC Tim Teter Dec 2 (AP)

Claude Code team verification practices (Addy Osmani, Claude Blog, 16 Nov 2026): ~90% of code written and reviewed by Claude; end-to-end tests first, verify skill, property tests (QuickCheck lineage), differential tests with the old system as oracle; human pulled in after three failed fix rounds; owner-written checks; a change can't modify the check that judges it; flaky-test rule; commit verification stamps including 'none'; one 'up to 10 points' grader figure

Y Combinator debate, Jacob Coxon vs Robin Hanson, on whether governments should substantially slow frontier AI (via StartupHub and BigGo Finance write-ups): Coxon's reported 4-5x Anthropic speedup doubling every 3 months to 100x in 2027, superintelligence ~2028, compute throttling and external safety cases; Hanson's diffusion history, capture argument, FAA-after-big-crashes line, ~$100B mandatory liability insurance; falsifiable bets (late-2027 hundredfold test; 50 real jobs with a camera; meet in three years); Amodei's opening-bell pacing pledge and Newport's IEEE Spectrum essay

dives.why_it_matters: Anyone exposed to Nvidia or following California AI policy: a state securities investigation lands just as Nvidia decides what risk factors go in a delayed quarterly filing, adding a non-federal investigator to a story the federal side is accused of ignoring.

dives.why_it_matters: Engineering leads facing the agent review bottleneck get a concrete, copyable practice for shifting humans from reading diffs to owning checks the change cannot edit.

dives.story: Coxon vs Hanson on slowing frontier AI
dives.why_it_matters: Policy-minded listeners get both sides of the slowdown argument reduced to testable claims, liability insurance versus compute throttling, as Congress and the labs' own CEOs talk about pacing.

concepts_taught: three verification types for agent-written code: end-to-end tests (hard to fool, unlike unit tests written from the agent's same misunderstanding), property-based tests (generated inputs free of the author's bias; round-trip, invariant, idempotency, equivalence), and differential tests (the old system as oracle for migrations)

lore.note: Ada's October position that an agent's pull request most needs a statement of intent written before the code developed: reading the Claude Code team's verification post, she said they had turned that statement into something that runs — owner-written checks the change cannot edit — and that she likes it better than her own version.
